name: Zoe Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do underground work in the city, so instead of climbing poles I'm usually down a vault under a street, splicing cable. A splice is where you join two big cables, and it's fiddly, careful work, layers of insulation, heat shrink, everything perfectly clean or it fails in a year. I like it because it's quiet down there and you can see your own good work. What I don't like is the traffic, the smell of the vaults in August, and people honking at our trucks like we chose to dig up their road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology fit into your day, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quite a lot, actually, probably more than most of my crew. I use an AI app on my phone every day to check splice kit instructions, look up cable specs, and I used it to study for my cable jointer upgrade. I'm the one who set up the crew's shared photo log so the office stops losing our paperwork. I live with my friend Priya, she's a designer, and she's way more worried about AI than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like, "Okay, so it's a better search engine with good marketing." I'd probably post a meme. People at work would tease me because I'm the one always showing them new apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed. I like the tools, they make my day easier. But my job's safe, my pay's the same, so it's hard to complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing exactly what I'm doing. Use the tools for the paperwork and the studying, keep at my jointer qualification, and keep pushing the company to buy the better gas detectors for the vaults instead of fancy software. My savings stay at about three months and grow slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little flat, like a concert that turns out to be just okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "a bit disappointed". What were you hoping for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the boring stuff gone. Permits, paperwork, the forms we fill out three times. And better safety, like sensors that warn you about gas in a vault before you go down. That's the AI I actually want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that disappointment change anything you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd keep using what works and keep my eye out. Maybe I'd spend a bit less time reading about it at night.

S0.say: I'd say it's a better search engine with good marketing, and probably post a meme. My crew would tease me because I'm always showing them new apps.
S0.think: Off the record I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the tools and they make my day easier. But my job and pay are safe, so it's hard to complain.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools for paperwork and study, keeps working toward her cable jointer qualification, and presses the company for better vault gas detectors. Lets her three months of savings grow slowly.
S0.feel: Calm, maybe a little flat, like a concert that turns out to be just okay.
S0.quote: It's a better search engine with good marketing.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is the crew's early adopter and is slightly let down by the plateau. What she wants from AI is concrete: less triple paperwork and better gas warnings in vaults. Her progressive streak shows in wanting safety spending over flashy software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if workers share in it. If machines make the job safer and faster, great, but the savings shouldn't all go to shareholders. I'd say that loudly, at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's mostly good. Underground splicing is hard to automate, the vaults are all different and cramped, so robots are years away from my bit. And I'm already comfortable with the tools, so I'd be useful in the change, not scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name forward for any pilot the company runs with new gear, and I'd join the union's technology committee to make sure the training's fair. I'd take a short course in using the new monitoring systems on the network. I might even help teach the guys on my crew who don't like screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, even a bit excited. It's the version where I get to help shape things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, my crew lead. He's brilliant with his hands but he still prints his emails. If the job becomes half tablet, he'd hate it, and he's got fifteen years to go. I'd want to make sure he isn't pushed out just because he types with one finger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Priya? You said she's more worried.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be hit harder than me, honestly. Design is exactly the kind of thing these tools do. We've joked that I'll be paying the rent and she'll be cooking. It's a joke, mostly.

S1.say: I'd say this is good if workers share in it. Safer, faster work is great, but the savings shouldn't all go to shareholders, and I'd say that loudly at the union and online.
S1.think: For me it's mostly good, because underground splicing in cramped, varied vaults is hard to automate. I'm already comfortable with the tools, so I'd be useful in the change rather than scared of it.
S1.do: Volunteers for any company pilot of new gear and joins the union's technology committee to keep training fair. Takes a short course on network monitoring systems and helps teach colleagues who dislike screens.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, because this is the version where she helps shape things.
S1.quote: He's brilliant with his hands but he still prints his emails.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe combines early-adopter confidence with solid union instincts: she wants the gains shared and older colleagues protected. She was quick to name Gary, her crew lead, as someone who'd struggle. Her joke about Priya cooking while she pays rent hints at real worry for her friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure it's owned by everyone, not five companies. If a machine can do all the work, the gains have to be shared, through taxes, a basic income, public ownership. I'd be at protests for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's unsettling. My whole edge has been being the one who's good with the new tools. If the tools can do the job themselves, being good at using them doesn't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd bank everything I could, cancel the gym and the streaming, and aim for six months of savings. I'd try to get onto whatever team the company forms to bring in and supervise the robots, because I know the network and I know the tech. And I'd be organising with the union for a basic income and for the grid to stay in public hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm in control, sort of, but it's moving faster than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "what I'm good at" might not count. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean I've always thought, the future's coming, I'll just be early. But two years means everyone's early and everyone's late at the same time. There's no head start to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you push the union and government to do in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guaranteed income, straight away, no forms three times. A say for workers in how the robots are used on the network, because safety on a live grid still matters. And taxing the companies that own these systems, properly.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment to make sure it's owned by everyone, not five companies. If machines do all the work, the gains have to be shared through taxes, basic income and public ownership, and I'd protest for that.
S2.think: Honestly it's unsettling, because my edge has been being good with new tools. If the tools can do the job themselves, that skill doesn't count for much.
S2.do: Cuts the gym and streaming and aims for six months of savings. Tries to join any company team that brings in and supervises the robots, while organising with the union for basic income and keeping the grid public.
S2.feel: Anxious; still in some control, but it's moving faster than she likes.
S2.quote: Two years means everyone's early and everyone's late at the same time.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario takes away Zoe's main advantage, being early to new tools, and she sees that clearly. Her politics sharpen into basic income and public ownership. She still acts fast, trying to get onto the team that runs the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to set the rules, so let's not waste them on arguing whether it's real. I'd want the union pushing for retraining funds and for workers on the boards of utility companies. I'd post about it, I'd go to meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, if I move early. Five years is enough time to get into robotics maintenance or grid control, and I'd be one of the first from my crew to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening course in robotics or automation at the technical college, probably two nights a week. I'd keep using AI every day and get better at it. And I'd keep my savings growing and help the union draft what we want in the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in a "let's go" way. It's a sprint, not a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be grabbing for anything. With five, I can pick, like choosing the course instead of taking whatever's open. And I'd have time to bring Gary along with me, which matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to safety. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been down a vault when the gas alarm went off. Took us forty seconds to get out and it felt like an hour. If robots go down there instead of people, honestly, that's a win, as long as the people get looked after.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to set the rules, so let's not waste them arguing whether it's real. I'd want the union pushing for retraining funds and workers on utility boards.
S3.think: I think I'd be fine if I move early. Five years is enough to get into robotics maintenance or grid control, and I'd be one of the first from my crew.
S3.do: Enrols in a two-night-a-week robotics or automation course at the technical college in the first year. Keeps sharpening her AI skills, keeps saving and helps the union draft its next contract demands.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in a "let's go" way, a sprint rather than a wall.
S3.quote: Took us forty seconds to get out and it felt like an hour.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Zoe moves from defence to choice: she'd pick her course and bring her crew lead along. The gas alarm story explains why she sees robots in vaults partly as a good thing. She's the rare person who sees a safety upside to losing her own tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to make it fair. Retraining for everyone, shorter work weeks, public ownership of the important stuff. I'd be fairly upbeat about it in public, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'd have time to train properly, maybe even a two-year diploma in electrical engineering technology, part-time. I'd come out the other side knowing both the old grid and the new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep splicing for a few years while studying part-time, then move into a role running or designing the automated systems. I'd keep active in the union, push for the shorter week. And I'd keep using AI every day, because whatever the job is in 2036, it'll be done with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now you'd be thirty-seven. What would you want to be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like the network control room, or training the people and the machines that work on the grid. Still in the trade, just with my hands on the controls instead of the cables. And a four-day week, if we fight for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this that you'd actually look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if people get shorter weeks and nobody gets thrown away. Honestly, a world where nobody has to go down a gassy vault in August sounds pretty good. The trick is making sure Gary and Priya are in it too.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to make it fair, with retraining for everyone, shorter weeks and public ownership of essentials. I'd be fairly upbeat in public.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd do well, with time to train properly, maybe a part-time electrical engineering technology diploma. I'd come out knowing both the old grid and the new machines.
S4.do: Keeps splicing for a few years while studying part-time, then moves into running or designing automated grid systems. Stays active in the union pushing for a shorter week and keeps using AI daily.
S4.quote: Still in the trade, just with my hands on the controls instead of the cables.
S4.fieldNote: This is the scenario Zoe could almost look forward to, as long as no one is left behind. Her plan is concrete: a part-time diploma and then the control room. She keeps tying her optimism to named people, Gary and Priya, which keeps it from sounding naive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away the one thing I'm good at, being early. What would help is a basic income that kicks in fast, and the union and workers having real power over how robots are used on the grid. Plus training that's actually free and actually at night, for people who still have to work during the day.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd be worried about besides myself. I'd be fine in most of these. It's the Garys, the people who've been doing this beautifully for thirty years and have never touched an app, that I'd lose sleep over.

headlineQuote: A world where nobody has to go down a gassy vault in August sounds pretty good.
portrait: Zoe Yilmaz is a 27-year-old underground cable splicer in the city who spends her days in street vaults joining high-voltage cables. She uses AI tools every day, set up her crew's photo log and lives with her friend Priya, a designer. She is pro-union and wants the gains from AI shared, and she worries more about colleagues like her crew lead Gary than about herself. She stays calm through the mild pictures, turns anxious when two-year AGI wipes out her head start, and becomes almost hopeful with a decade to train for the control room.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it takes away her one real advantage, being early with new tools.
whatWouldHelp: A fast basic income, real worker power over how robots are used on the grid, and free evening training for people who still work days.
